title: Encode and Test the Escalation Branch
scenario: It is 6:38 AM. Today's risk record says ERCOT escalates - but a branch you have only run once is a branch you have not tested. Route three mornings through the fork, including the exact-boundary case, and log each decision so the audit trail shows why each brief went where it went.
input:
Escalation rule (Threshold Policy v1.0.0): a day-over-day move of 12 percent OR MORE requires manager approval before the brief is sent. Escalated mornings route to approval-route; all others route to routine-update-path.

Three mornings to route (biggest day-over-day move on the map that day):
day-1 (today): 13.3 percent (ERCOT)
day-2: 12.0 percent (SPP)
day-3: 11.9 percent (ERCOT)
instructions: For each day, record the biggest move as a plain number in biggestMovePct.
Apply the rule: 12 or more means escalationRequired is true.
Watch the boundary: day-2 is exactly 12.0 - the rule says OR MORE.
Set route to approval-route or routine-update-path accordingly.
Return a JSON array with one object per day, then validate.
copilotPrompt: Route three days through an escalation branch. Rule: a move of 12 percent or more sets escalationRequired true and route approval-route; otherwise escalationRequired false and route routine-update-path. Days: day-1 13.3, day-2 12.0, day-3 11.9. Return a JSON array of { day, biggestMovePct, escalationRequired, route }.
successMessage: Decision log built. The fork is tested, boundary included, and every evaluation is on the record.

sections.title: A branch is a condition someone owns
sections.body: This fork does not invent a rule - it applies the Threshold Policy's 12-or-more escalation rule. The decision step evaluates; the policy decides. Keeping those separate is why the rule can change without rewiring the workflow.

sections.title: Boundaries are where automations go wrong
sections.body: Is exactly 12.0 an escalation? The policy says OR MORE, so yes. Off-by-one boundary readings are among the most common automation bugs, which is why you test the exact-boundary case on purpose.

sections.title: Every decision gets logged
sections.body: The fork produces no brief and no price - its product IS the routing record. If day-3 is questioned next week, the log shows: biggest move 11.9, threshold 12, routine path. No log, no answer.

sections.title: Testing a branch means multiple cases
sections.body: One morning cannot prove a fork works. You route three: clearly over, exactly at, and just under the threshold. That trio is the minimum honest test of any threshold branch, in any tool.

fieldGuide.meaning: Which morning this decision applies to.
fieldGuide.hint: One object per day: day-1, day-2, day-3.

fieldGuide.meaning: The biggest day-over-day percent move that morning.
fieldGuide.hint: A plain number from the input. 12.0 can be written as 12.

fieldGuide.meaning: Whether the rule fires for this morning.
fieldGuide.hint: true when the move is 12 or more. Exactly 12 counts.
approval-route when escalationRequired is true, else routine-update-path.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You'd apply the rule - auto-approve if within tolerance, otherwise send to a person - so obvious cases don't wait on a human.

tools.powerAutomate: 'Condition' -> either auto-complete or 'Start and wait for an approval'
tools.zapier: 'Filter'/'Paths' that auto-pass clean cases and route the rest

takeaway.heading: Decision log built
points: You encoded the fork as an explicit condition referencing the governed threshold, not a judgment call.
You proved the boundary: exactly 12.0 escalates, because the rule says OR MORE.
All three evaluations are logged, so 'why did day-3 skip approval?' has an on-the-record answer.
Today (day-1) routes to Approval Route - that handoff is the Approval Route task; day-3 shows why the quiet path also needs a log.
The workflow can now route the morning brief through the correct approval path.
